Yes — horizontal giving is the second major dimension of forgiveness in the NT corpus, named in group 5377-002 (11 verses) and across multiple commands:

**The commanded giving of forgiveness:**
- Mat 18:35 — "forgive your brother from your heart." The giving is commanded, heart-level, and addressed to a specific relational other ("your brother").
- Luk 17:3-4 — "if he repents, forgive him... seven times in the day... you must forgive him." The giving is repeated, responsive to verbal repentance, and without accumulating limit.
- Mar 11:25 — "whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone." The giving of forgiveness is embedded in the prayer-posture — the regular rhythmic context.
- Luk 11:4 — "forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us." The giving is described as the accompanying act that grounds the request for received forgiveness — the structural congruence (F-003).

**How the giving operates:** OBS-064-026 — "the inner-being act is a volitional release — choosing to no longer hold a legitimate claim." The giving operates as a deliberate inner decision to release what is legitimately held. The giving is not a natural impulse (like love or compassion) but a commanded volitional act with a cost.

Yes. Group 5470-002 (charizō as human forgiving act — 8 relevant verses): Eph 4:32 (anchor): "forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you." Group 889-003 (chen as gracious character quality): Pro 31:30 (anchor). Speech-grace (SD022: gracious words, speech seasoned with grace) as a further giving mode.

Yes — the human-to-human giving direction is well-evidenced, primarily through the splanchnizō Gospels pattern (human subjects), the sumpatheō/sumpaschō vocabulary, and the eleēmosunē evidence.

**Luke 10:33 — the Good Samaritan:** The most explicit human-to-human compassion-giving in the data. The Samaritan is splanchnizō toward the wounded man and extends an extraordinary investment of care: binding wounds, providing transport, shelter, and ongoing financial provision. This is compassion-giving in its fullest and most complete form — extending across cultural distance, at personal cost, to a stranger.

**Luke 15:20 — the father of the prodigal:** Splanchnizō in a relational-moral context. The father's compassion-movement produces immediate, uninhibited action: running, embracing, kissing, restoring to full sonship. This is compassion-giving within a broken relational bond — the restoration of what was lost.

**Matt 18:27 — the king in the parable:** Splanchnizō producing release of debt. Compassion-giving in a judicial-moral context — mercy rather than judgment, at great personal financial cost to the king.

**Heb 10:34 — sumpatheō in the community:** The readers showing compassion (sumpatheō) to those in prison, expressed through the joyful acceptance of property plundering. This is participatory compassion-giving in the context of persecution — sharing in another's loss as an act of genuine solidarity.

**G1654 eleēmosunē:** Almsgiving as the normalised social form of compassion-giving. Matt 6:2-4 establishes the manner: privately, from inner purity, not for display. Luke 11:41 — "give as alms those things that are within" — grounds the outer act in the inner quality.

Yes. The horizontal giving of fellowship is evidenced in multiple modes.

**Proclamatory giving:** 1Jo 1:3 — *that which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us* — the one who has received fellowship extends it to others through proclamation. The act of proclamation is the act of fellowship-extension.

**Mutual support giving:** Ecc 4:10 — *one will lift up his fellow* — the person in fellowship gives support to the fallen companion. Fellowship is expressed as active giving of support.

**Companionship-offering:** Psa 119:63 — the psalmist's self-positioning among those who fear God represents a willingness to give and receive companionship within the fear-of-God community.

Human-to-human giving of goodness is evidenced in four forms: (1) Instruction and edification — Rom 15:14 ("full of goodness... able to instruct one another"): the goodness-filled person extends goodness toward others through teaching and building up. (2) Kindness as relational disposition — Col 3:12 (put on chrēstotēs as garment): the deliberate expression of generosity of spirit toward others in the community. (3) Justice and right action — Mic 6:8 ("to do justice"): goodness extended toward others as the active practice of just treatment. (4) Covenantal kindness — the tov vocabulary in its relational register covers loyalty and steadfast faithfulness in human relationships, paralleling the divine hesed-goodness pattern. Each of these is an extension of inner goodness toward another person. (OBS-067-OBS-025, OBS-067-OBS-027, OBS-067-OBS-039, SBF-067-Q039)

Love as given outward is the primary ethical direction of the commandment structure: love your neighbour (Lev 19:18), love your enemy (Mat 5:44), love one another (Joh 13:34). The giving of love reaches its maximum in Joh 15:13 (OBS-103-125) — 'greater love has no one than this: that someone lay down his life/soul for his friends.' The gift of the soul is love's outer limit. The giving-forms span: chesed as daily covenantal faithfulness given to the covenant-partner (OBS-103-089); agapē given to the enemy against natural preference (OBS-103-143); phileō given as warmth within the community (OBS-103-119); rachamim given as compassion toward the suffering (OBS-103-105). Love-as-given is the primary ethical form in which the inner orientation is concretely actualised.

Yes — human-to-human mercy extension is evidenced in: Mat 18:33 (mercy-obligation on the one who received mercy, OBS-111-055); Dan 4:27 (showing mercy to the oppressed, OBS-111-062); Jam 2:13 (one who has shown mercy, OBS-111-070); Mat 5:7 (the merciful — those whose inner character extends mercy, OBS-111-032). The extension is toward those in a weaker or guilty position — the oppressed (Dan 4:27), the debtor (Mat 18:33). OBS-111-032, OBS-111-055, OBS-111-062.

The substitutionary group (Isa 53:5) involves the Servant's crushing producing outcomes for others — the nearest instance of contrition-vocabulary being "extended" toward another. However, this is not interpersonal contrition (person A being contrite toward person B) but vicarious crushing (the Servant's crushing producing peace and healing in the community). Genuine interpersonal contrition — being contrite toward another human one has wronged — is implied in Psa 51's context (David's sin against Bathsheba and Uriah) but the verses in the registry focus on the vertical dimension. OBS-030-041, OBS-030-042.

Yes — richly evidenced. Ecc 4:10 (the friend who lifts when one falls), Psa 119:63 (companion of God-fearers as community formation), Mal 2:14 (covenant companion), Isa 1:23 (companion of thieves as moral-formation warning), 2Cor 1:7 (sharing comfort proportionate to sharing suffering). OBS-062-050, OBS-062-054, OBS-062-057, OBS-062-031.

Yes — commanded horizontal forgiveness is richly evidenced. Mat 18:35 (forgive from the heart), Luk 17:3-4 (if your brother sins, rebuke him; if he repents, forgive him — seven times a day), Mat 18:22 (seventy times seven). Eph 4:32 ("forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you"). OBS-064-031.

Yes — the horizontal giving of covenant is evidenced in person-to-person covenant traditions. (1) Covenant of friendship: 3304-004 (OBS-034-049) — karat berit between persons as a relational act of committed loyalty, given to another person. The Jonathan-David covenant (implied by 3304-004's framing) is the giving of covenant-loyalty to another person — a genuine act of self-giving in the horizontal register. (2) Marriage covenant: H1285 1a5 (OBS-034-009, 765-005 direction) — the marriage covenant is the giving of covenantal commitment to a spouse — an act of solemn self-binding toward another person. (3) Firm covenant with community: Neh 9:38 (OBS-034-037) — the community leaders extend covenant-commitment to the whole people by putting their names on the sealed document — a giving of formal commitment to and on behalf of others. (4) Oaths given to another: H7650 (OBS-034-017) — swearing an oath to another person as the giving of binding commitment: the person extends their covenantal word to another as a gift of reliable promise.

Yes — extensively. Human-to-human extension of peace: (1) The greeting-blessing (H7965K, 2511-001): 1Sa 25:6 — the triple sha.lom blessing extended by messengers to Nabal; (2) Seeking the welfare of others: Est 10:3 (Mordecai seeking the sha.lom of his people), Jer 29:7 (seeking the welfare of the exile city for others' benefit); (3) Peacemaking: Jam 3:18 — the peacemaker sows righteousness in peace; (4) G1514 eirēneuō: Rom 12:18 — "as far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all"; (5) Apostolic peace-blessing: Rom 1:7 and all Pauline letter openings — "grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ" — the apostle extending peace in blessing; (6) Speaking peace: Psa 122:8 — "for my brothers and companions' sake I will say, 'Peace be within you'" — peace spoken toward community.

The classified corpus is primarily God-to-human and human-to-God; human-to-human giving in the inner-being register is less evidenced. Group 872-005 (human self-giving) contains human-to-community instances: Neh 7:70-72 (heads of fathers' houses giving to community work — OBS-060-022), Num 5:7 (giving restitution to the wronged). These are human-to-another-human giving instances within the community, expressing inner orientation toward the community. However, the anchor verses (Job 1:21, Isa 50:6) are primarily human-to-God or human covenantal-obedience, not human-to-human. The human-to-human direction in the classified data is present but thin at the anchor level, making a full answer to this prompt partial.

Yes, extensively in groups 1601 and 1200. Hatred is extended as an ongoing orientation shaping all interaction: Gen 37:4 — brothers give hatred to Joseph through their inability to speak peacefully. 2Sa 13:22 — Absalom gives his settled hatred to Amnon through years of silent enmity before acting. Pro 26:24 — the hater gives hatred through disguised speech. The giving of person-directed hatred is not typically a discrete act but an ongoing orientation.

Yes. Contempt is given in multiple contexts: the comfortable giving contempt to the suffering (Job 12:5), the nations giving contempt to Israel (group 1277-001), the proud giving contempt to the righteous (Psa 123:4), priests giving contempt to God through hollow worship (Mal 1:6-12).

Yes, in the receiving register. Job 19:19: "all my intimate friends abhor me" — the intimate friends give abhorrence to Job. Isa 49:7: "abhorred by the nation" — the nation gives abhorrence to the Servant. The giving of abhorrence is documented through what the recipient experiences.
Yes. Groups 6966-001, 6967-001 document the giving of cruelty: the cruel person gives cruelty through their conduct toward others. Group 1775-002 documents it from the receiving side.

M06-E is the receiving sub-group — it documents what is given to the person rather than what the person gives. The one verse that speaks of giving-reproach-to-another as something to be avoided is Psa 15:3: "nor takes up a reproach against his friend" — the righteous person is characterised by not wielding reproach against others.
The giving of the adversary relationship is structural — another party positions themselves in opposition. The human giving in M06-F is the taking-up of the adversary posture.

Yes. The nations give malice to Israel: Ammon (Eze 25:6), the Philistines (Eze 25:15), Edom (Eze 36:5). The giving is documented through the soul's rejoicing in Israel's destruction and the purposive acts of destruction.

Yes — Mat 5:7 (Group 1631): "blessed are the merciful"; Mat 18:33 (Group 1630): "should you not have had mercy on your fellow servant?" — human mercy-giving is explicitly commanded and required.

Yes — extensively. The agathopoieō compound family (Group 1093) is entirely about human doing of good toward others: "love your enemies and do good" (Luk 6:35 — Group 1093); "do good to those who do good to you" and beyond (Group 1093).

**[A1 — God Righteousness]** God's righteousness is not given by one human to another — it is the divine standard. S.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** Yes — righteousness flows outward to others in multiple modes: guiding the neighbor (Pro 12:26), caring for animals (Pro 12:10), delivering from oppression (Jer 22:3), dealing fairly with workers (Mat 20:4), interceding for the community (Abraham's intercession for Sodom, Gen 18:23–28, VSG M26-A2-015). The righteous person's inner condition generates a giving movement toward others.

**[B — Moral Uprightness]** Yes — upright speech is given to others: "he who walks righteously and speaks uprightly" (Isa 33:15) — the uprightness of speech is expressed toward those who hear. "Whoever speaks the truth gives honest evidence" (Pro 12:17, VSG M26-A2-011) — truth-speaking is a giving act toward those who need honest testimony.

**[C — Justification]** Justification as such is not given by one human to another — it is God's exclusive act. However, the human judicial act of vindicating the innocent (947-002: Deu 25:1; 2Sa 15:4) is a human-to-human expression of the justification principle. The human judge who acquits the innocent is extending a form of the justification-act toward the person before them.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** Yes — the commissioned human avenger (Rom 13:4) extends justice toward wrongdoers on behalf of the wronged. This is a human-to-human giving of justice — the authority serves others by executing the retribution due to wrongdoers. Moses avenging the oppressed Israelite (Act 7:24, VSG 945-001) is a human giving of protective justice toward the vulnerable.

**[E — Condemnation]** Yes — the human judge extends condemnation toward the guilty (Mat 12:37; Luk 6:37). This can be legitimate (passing righteous judgment) or illegitimate (condemning the righteous, Pro 17:15). The human-to-human extension of condemnation is a reality in the cluster — and it requires careful scrutiny because it is susceptible to corruption.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** Yes — the human judge who "reckons" the worth of a case and passes verdict (947-002: the judges who decide between persons, Deu 25:1) extends the reckoning act toward others. Paul's instruction to "consider" others (implied in the adiakritos material, G0087) — impartial assessment of others is a giving of honest moral reckoning toward them.

**[CLUSTER — T4.3]** E. The giving interface is present in A2 (outward-flowing righteousness), B (truth-speaking to others), C-adjacent (human judicial vindication), D (commissioned justice), E (human judgment), and F (impartial assessment of others). The cluster reveals that righteousness in the human person is inherently other-directed — it reaches toward others in giving modes across multiple forms.
VCG01 (Pro 16:23): wisdom guides the mouth — speech as the giving form. VCG04 (froneō, Phil 2:2-5): shared orientation as communal giving. The wise person's life and speech give wisdom to others.
VCG07 (dialegō): sustained Scripture-based engagement with others — understanding given through teaching and argumentation.
VCG06 (Pro 10:14): "lips of the wise spread knowledge" — human-to-human transmission as teaching. VCG08: testimony-assertion as giving conviction to others.
VCG04 (cha.shav assessments): human assessments shared in discourse. VCG06 (a.rum): prudent person manages what they give in social contexts.
VCG04 (2Sa 16:23): counsel as the primary giving form — the counselor gives their inner wisdom to the counselee.
M15-F's meditative activity is primarily inward. The wisdom produced can be shared, but the sharing belongs to other clusters.
M15-G does not have a primary human-to-human giving mode. Thought-content is interior.
VCG02 (Col 4:6): gracious, timely, appropriate speech as the primary giving form. VCG01 (1Cor 14:19): intelligible speech that reaches the inner person of the hearer.
Not evidenced in BOUNDARY's single active verse.

The positive register of merimnaō (2709-003) shows directed care extended by one person toward another: Paul's merimna for the churches (2Cor 11:28), Timothy's concern for the Philippians (Phili 2:20), mutual care in the body (1Cor 12:25). The anxiety-faculty, rightly directed, is the vehicle of love given to others.

Two distinct giving modes: positive (parakaleō — encouragement given to the discouraged: 1Th 5:14) and negative (discouragement inflicted — athumeō from provocation Col 3:21; ka.eh disheartened by false prophets Eze 13:22). The characteristic can be given in its negative form — one person can impose discouragement on another.

Yes — in three forms: (1) Forgiveness: charizō group 5470-002 (Eph 4:32; Col 3:13; 2Cor 2:7; 2Cor 2:10) — the human extending grace-forgiveness to another. (2) Generosity: cha.nan group 984-001 (Psa 37:21; 37:26: "he is ever lending generously, and his children become a blessing") — the gracious-generous person giving to others. (3) Priestly/prophetic blessing of others: ba.rakh group 1299-003 (Num 6:24; Gen 14:19; Gen 9:26) — the human mediating divine grace-blessing over another. (4) Chen as character quality: group 889-003 (Pro 1:9; 3:22; 4:9) — the gracious person whose wisdom-conduct produces grace in community.

Yes — through good action and good speech: ya.tav group 632-002 (the pattern of doing good toward others); Pro 15:2 (632-002 — the tongue of the wise commending knowledge); the communal approval texts (632-003 — goodness of judgment shared in community).

M46-D is constituted by giving: the widow giving all her living (Luk 21:3-4), Zacchaeus distributing half his goods (Luk 19:8), the Macedonian churches giving from extreme poverty (2Cor 8:2), the apostles enriching many while being poor (2Cor 6:10). The act of material giving is the primary external expression of M46-D's inner postures.

Giving in M46-B appears through its distortion: the rich man of 2Sa 12:4 who was "unwilling" (lo a.vah cha.mal) to give from his own abundance — the failure of giving reveals the hardness. The command to give to the poor in Luk 14:13 and Luk 18:22 is precisely the command that the hardened wealthy person cannot easily comply with.

Pro 11:25 (via da.shen — "whoever brings blessing will be enriched") evidences the giving pattern of M46-C: the one who blesses others receives enrichment as consequence. The generous orientation produces the M46-C enrichment pattern.

M01-A's ethical dimension involves extending the effects of fear toward others: the God-fearer treats the vulnerable justly (Lev 19:14; 25:43) and extends generosity (Lev 25:36-37). But the fear itself is not "given" to another — it is the inner posture that governs the person's treatment of others. The one quasi-exception is the pedagogical dimension: the psalmist offers to "teach fear of the Lord" (Psa 34:11) — fear being transmitted through instruction and example.

M01-B's "do not fear" command shows one person extending release from fear toward another: David to Mephibosheth (2Sa 9:7), Elisha to his servant (2Ki 6:16), Jesus to the disciples (Mar 4:40; Mat 28:10). The characteristic being extended is not fear itself but the command and ground that releases fear.

M01-F-VCG-05 (pastoral anxiety) shows one person extending concern toward another: Paul's anticipatory dread for his churches (2Cor 12:20; Gal 4:11) flows from his care. The anxiety is in Paul, motivated by love for others — a one-directional giving of concerned attention.

Fear is not typically "given" as a gift from one person to another. The human-to-human dimension of M01 is primarily indirect: fear of God produces just treatment of others (M01-A), the command to release fear is extended from one to another (M01-B-VCG-06), and pastoral anxiety flows from loving concern (M01-F-VCG-05).

Yes. The provocation corpus (M02-D-VCG-02) evidences deliberate human-to-human provocation: Peninnah deliberately and repeatedly provoking Hannah (1Sa 1:6–7 / M02-D-VCG-02). The action-driving corpus (M02-B-VCG-02) shows anger from one person directed against another and producing outward action: Eliab's anger against David (1Sa 17:28); Saul's anger against Jonathan (1Sa 20:30); officials' anger against Jeremiah (Jer 37:15).

Strife and quarrel (M02-F-VCG-01) are definitionally person-to-person: eris (quarrel) as an inner disposition that "generates hostile conflict in relationships" (Gal 5:20).

Yes. Several modes of grief extended person-to-person. (1) Empathic solidarity: weeping with those who weep is commanded (Rom 12:15 — M03-A-VCG-05); this is the volitional act of entering into another's grief as a form of love. (2) Prophetic compassion: the prophet weeps on behalf of a people or nation (Jer 9:1 — M03-A-VCG-04 anchor; 2Ki 8:11-12); this is grief extended from prophet to people as an act of identification. (3) Apostolic pastoral grief: Paul's grief over the Corinthians (2Cor 2:4; 7:11 — M03-C-VCG-02) and anticipatory grief over unrepentant members (2Cor 12:21) shows pastoral grief directed toward a community. (4) Apostolic travail: Gal 4:19 (M03-E-VCG-02) — Paul's apostolic travail-grief directed toward the Galatians as a form of love-anguish.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, partially. VCG-03 (relational and natural gladness) contains Pro 23:24–25 (father's exultation over a righteous son; mother called to rejoice at her child's goodness). Isa 9:3 shows the people glad "as when they divide the spoil" — communal exultation that involves persons sharing in a collective triumph. Song 1:4 shows relational exultation directed toward the beloved king. Isa 66:10 calls "all who love Jerusalem" to rejoice with her.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, extensively. (1) **M04-B-VCG-04** — parental joy over wise children (Pro 10:1; 15:20; 23:24–25; 29:3; 29:6); Deu 24:5 (husband making wife glad — a legal provision for Joy directed toward a spouse); (2) **M04-D** — sunchairo throughout: the shepherd calling neighbours to co-rejoice (Luk 15:6, 9); co-rejoicing in the body (1Cor 12:26); Paul rejoicing with the Philippians (Phili 2:17–18); (3) **Pauline relational joy** (M04-C-VCG-03) — Paul's pastoral joy over communities (1Th 3:9; Phili 4:1; 1Th 2:19–20; 3Jo 3–4; Phili 2:2); (4) **News-bearing joy** — Luk 1:14 (Zechariah's joy to be shared with many at John's birth); Act 15:3 (Barnabas and Paul bringing great joy to the brothers through news of Gentile conversions); (5) **Act 2:46** — the community receiving food with glad and generous hearts, expressing outward-directed joy.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Yes: Act 16:34 (the jailer's rejoicing encompasses his entire household — the characteristic radiates from the newly-believing person into the communal relational network); Act 5:41 (the apostles rejoicing together — the characteristic is shared among the community, extending from each to the others in the shared experience); Luk 1:44 (the baby in Elizabeth's womb leaping for joy at Mary's greeting — Suffering-Joy radiating across the relational encounter of two pregnant women in vulnerable circumstances); Luk 15:6, 9 (M04-D adjacent — the shepherd/woman calling neighbours to co-rejoice, but the Spirit-joy quality of the lost-found is adjacent to this characteristic's intensity).

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. (1) **Good words and news** — M04-O-VCG-01: Pro 12:25 ("a good word makes him glad") — the apt word extended by one person toward another; Pro 15:23 ("to make an apt answer is a joy to a man") — the speaker extends Gladness through speech; Isa 52:7's good-news herald brings Gladness to Zion; 2Sa 18:27's "good man comes with good news" — character and news combined in relational extension; (2) **Relational loyalty and goodness** — 1Sa 25:15 ("the men were very good to us") — David's men extending practical goodness to Nabal's servants; 1Sa 19:4 (Jonathan testifying of David's good deeds to Saul — relational advocacy); 1Sa 24:19 (Saul acknowledging David's relational goodness); (3) **Testimony of God's good hand** — Neh 2:18 (Nehemiah sharing the testimony of God's good hand, which motivates the community's resolve).
